label: Decision Theory: Loss, Risk, Admissibility and Minimax — mastery test (unseen)

items.stem: The risk of a decision rule δ is:
options: A single number summarising its quality
The loss incurred at the observed sample
The expected loss averaged over a prior for θ
The expected loss over the sampling distribution, as a function of θ
items.explanation: R(θ, δ) = E_θ[L(θ, δ(X))] — an expectation over the DATA with θ held fixed, so it is a function of θ. The averaged-over-a-prior option describes Bayes risk, which is a single number, and the loss at the observed sample is the loss itself, before any expectation is taken at all.

items.stem: A decision rule δ₂ is inadmissible if:
options: Some rule has risk no larger at every θ and strictly smaller at some θ
Its risk is not constant in θ
It is not a Bayes rule for any prior
Its worst-case risk exceeds that of some other rule
items.explanation: That is the definition of being dominated. Non-constant risk is irrelevant to admissibility, and having a larger worst case than another rule only means you are not minimax — a rule can lose on the worst case and still be admissible, because the other rule may be worse elsewhere.

items.stem: Under squared-error loss, the risk of an estimator equals:
options: Its variance plus its squared bias
Its variance minus its squared bias
items.explanation: Risk under squared error is the mean squared error, which decomposes as variance + bias². It reduces to the variance alone only when the estimator is unbiased — which is why the risk of the sample proportion is just p(1−p)/n.

items.stem: A minimax decision rule is one that minimises:
options: The average risk over a prior
The risk at the true parameter value
The maximum risk over all θ
items.explanation: Minimax minimises sup_θ R(θ, δ) — the worst case. Minimising the average risk over a prior gives the Bayes rule, and 'the risk at the true parameter value' is not a usable criterion, since the true value is unknown — that impossibility is the reason the two collapses of the risk curve exist at all.

items.stem: For X ~ Bin(n, p), the worst-case risk of the maximum likelihood estimator p̂ = X/n under squared-error loss is:
items.explanation: p̂ is unbiased, so its risk is Var(p̂) = p(1−p)/n, which is largest at p = 0.5 where p(1−p) = 1/4. The worst case is therefore 1/(4n) — for n = 9 that is 1/36 = 0.0278.
items.check: Maximise p(1−p) first: it peaks at 1/4 when p = 0.5. Then divide by n.

items.stem: Which relation is used in practice to establish that a rule is minimax?
options: A Bayes rule with constant risk is minimax
Every minimax rule is a Bayes rule for the uniform prior
An unbiased rule with minimum variance is minimax
items.explanation: This is the relation that does the work: it converts minimising a supremum into choosing a prior that flattens the risk curve. Admissibility does not imply minimaxity, the least favourable prior is generally not uniform, and minimum-variance unbiasedness is a separate criterion entirely.

items.stem: For X ~ Bin(16, p) under squared-error loss, the minimax estimator of p and its risk are:
items.explanation: With a = √n/2 = 2, the estimator is (x + a)/(n + 2a) = (x + 2)/20 and the constant risk is 1/(4(1 + √n)²) = 1/(4 × 25) = 0.0100. The value 0.0156 is 1/64, which is the MLE's worst case for n = 16, and (x + 2)/18 has the wrong denominator — it must be n + 2a, not n + a.
items.check: Denominator n + 2a = 16 + 4 = 20, and 1/(4(1+4)²) = 1/100. Both must be right for the option to be.

items.stem: The rule 'ignore the data and always report the constant c' under squared-error loss is:
options: Inadmissible, because it uses no data
Minimax, because its risk is constant
Admissible, because its risk is zero at θ = c
Neither admissible nor minimax, because its risk is unbounded
items.explanation: Its risk is (θ − c)², which is zero at θ = c, so no rule can have risk no larger everywhere and strictly smaller somewhere — it is admissible. Its risk is not constant and is unbounded, so it is certainly not minimax. This is the standard demonstration that admissibility is a weak criterion.

items.stem: Consider the following statements about the relations between Bayes, minimax and admissible rules.
items.explanation: A and D hold. B is false without a uniqueness qualifier — a minimax rule need not be admissible, though a UNIQUE one is. C is false too: a Bayes rule is minimax only if its risk is constant, which most Bayes rules are not.
statements: A unique Bayes rule is admissible.
A Bayes rule whose risk is constant in θ is minimax.

A.why: The uniqueness is essential; without it the implication can fail.

B.why: Minimaxity concerns the worst case only; a unique minimax rule is admissible, but not every one.

C.why: Only if its risk is constant. Most Bayes rules have risk that varies with θ.

D.why: A maximum is at least an average, applied once — and the prior is then the least favourable prior.

items.stem: For X ~ Bin(9, p), the risk of the MLE and that of the minimax estimator are equal at:
items.explanation: Set p(1−p)/9 = 1/64, giving p² − p + 9/64 = 0 and p = (1 ± √0.4375)/2 = 0.1693 and 0.8307. The pair 0.2 and 0.8 is the answer for n = 16, where the equation is p² − p + 0.16 = 0 — a genuine result for the wrong sample size.
items.check: The two roots must be symmetric about 0.5, since p(1−p) is. And at p = 0.5 the MLE's risk is 0.0278 against 0.0156, so they are certainly not equal there.

items.stem: For a normal mean with known variance σ², the estimator x̄ has risk σ²/n at every θ. It follows that x̄ is:
options: Minimax only if the prior is normal
Not minimax, because its risk does not depend on θ
Minimax, because its risk is constant
items.explanation: For the normal location problem with known variance and squared-error loss, x̄ has constant risk σ²/n, and the minimax lower bound for this problem is also σ²/n (for example, obtained as the limit of Bayes risks under increasingly diffuse normal priors). Hence x̄ attains the minimax bound. Constant risk alone is NOT sufficient to prove minimaxity: a constant-risk rule can have a larger worst-case risk than another rule, as the separate example in this pool illustrates.

items.stem: Match the criterion in List I with its definition in List II.
items.explanation: Risk is the expected loss over the data for fixed θ; Bayes risk averages that over a prior; a minimax rule minimises the maximum risk; an admissible rule is one that nothing dominates. Each wrong option moves at least two pairs, so the mapping must be checked rather than inferred from one entry.
items.check: Separate the two that are quantities (risk, Bayes risk) from the two that are properties of a rule (minimax, admissible), and the mapping halves.
pairs: I. Minimises the maximum risk over θ
II. Not dominated by any other rule
III. Expected loss over the data, for a fixed θ
IV. Risk averaged over a prior for θ

items.stem: For X ~ Bin(4, p) under squared-error loss, the minimax value is:
items.explanation: The minimax value is 1/(4(1 + √n)²) = 1/(4 × 9) = 1/36 = 0.0278. The value 0.0625 is 1/16, which is the MLE's worst case 1/(4n) for n = 4 — a correct quantity for the wrong question, and the distractor most candidates pick.
items.check: The minimax value must be strictly below the MLE's worst case of 1/(4n) = 0.0625, so 0.0625 cannot be the answer and 0.1250 is larger still.

items.stem: In decision-theoretic language, a test of hypotheses uses the action space {0, 1} and 0–1 loss. Its risk at a particular θ is:
options: The probability of an error at that θ
items.explanation: With 0–1 loss the expected loss is the probability of taking the wrong action: the probability of a type I error for θ in H₀, and of a type II error for θ in H₁. Size is the supremum of the first over H₀ and power is one minus the second, so both are features of that risk function rather than the risk itself.

items.stem: Consider the following statements about admissibility.
items.explanation: A, C and D hold. B is false: the maximum likelihood estimator of a normal mean VECTOR is inadmissible once the dimension is three or more, which is the most famous inadmissibility result in the subject.
statements: A rule that ignores the data entirely can be admissible.
The maximum likelihood estimator is admissible in every problem.
An unbiased estimator need not be admissible.

A.why: Its risk is zero at one parameter value, so nothing can dominate it.

B.why: For a normal mean vector in dimension three or more, a shrinkage estimator dominates it everywhere.

C.why: Unbiasedness is a constraint, not a guarantee of undominatedness.

D.why: A constant rule is admissible and its worst-case risk is unbounded.

items.stem: The least favourable prior in a minimax problem is best described as:
options: The prior against which the best achievable Bayes risk is largest
The prior that a cautious statistician would actually believe
The uniform prior over the parameter space
The prior that minimises the Bayes risk of the minimax rule
items.explanation: It names the hardest problem in the family — the prior maximising the minimum achievable Bayes risk — and solving that one problem solves the minimax problem. It is a device rather than a belief, and it is generally not uniform: for the binomial problem it is Beta(√n/2, √n/2).

items.stem: Under the loss L(θ, a) = 3(θ − a) for a < θ and (a − θ) for a ≥ θ, the Bayes rule is:
items.explanation: This is weighted absolute-error loss with k₁ = 3 for under-estimation and k₂ = 1 for over-estimation, and the Bayes rule is the k₁/(k₁ + k₂) quantile — here 3/4. Under-estimating is the costlier error, so the estimate must move ABOVE the median; the 0.25 quantile is the answer with the weights transposed, which is the error the options are built around.
items.check: Equal weights must give the median, and 1/(1+1) = 1/2 ✓. Then check the direction: costlier under-estimation pushes the estimate up.

items.stem: A rule has perfectly constant risk σ² for every θ, and is not minimax. Which explanation is correct?
options: Constant risk is sufficient for minimaxity, so the premise is impossible
Constant risk is only sufficient alongside the rule being a Bayes rule, and this one is not
The risk must be constant AND small for the rule to be minimax
Minimaxity requires the risk to be constant and the loss to be bounded
items.explanation: The relation has two conditions: a BAYES rule with constant risk is minimax. 'Always report x₁' has constant risk σ², is flat as anything, and is dominated by x̄ for every n > 1 — so flatness alone proves nothing. The third option is not a theorem, because 'small' is not a defined condition, and boundedness of the loss is not required.

items.stem: For X ~ Bin(25, p), by what factor does the MLE's worst-case risk exceed the minimax value?
items.explanation: The MLE's worst case is 1/(4n) = 1/100 = 0.0100 and the minimax value is 1/(4(1 + √n)²) = 1/(4 × 36) = 1/144 = 0.006944. The ratio is 144/100 = 1.44. In general the factor is (1 + √n)²/n, which equals 1.78 for n = 9 and approaches 1 as n grows — the minimax rule's advantage is a small-sample phenomenon.
items.check: The general factor is (1+√n)²/n = (1 + 1/√n)². For n = 25 that is (1 + 0.2)² = 1.44.

items.stem: Two rules have identical risk at every value of θ. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Each dominates the other, so both are inadmissible
They must be the same rule
Neither dominates the other, so the admissibility of one says nothing about the other
items.explanation: Domination requires risk no larger everywhere AND strictly smaller somewhere; identical risk fails the second condition in both directions, so neither dominates. They need not be the same rule — two different rules can be risk-equivalent — and whether either is minimax depends on whether that common risk has the smallest achievable supremum, which identical risk alone does not establish.
